title: Vaisakhi, 1699: the call
hook: before a great crowd the Guru draws his sword and asks who will give their head

segments.voice: Yesterday, a court of poets at Anandpur, the Dasam Granth, and a Sufi saint at Bhangani. Your line was pen and sword.

Spring, 1699, at Anandpur: the harvest festival of Vaisakhi. The Guru has sent word across Punjab and beyond: come. And they come, tens of thousands, tradition says, filling the hillside, expecting hymns, a festival, a blessing. This whole week has been building to this one morning: three companions who did not bend, a Guru who gave his head in Chandni Chowk for another's faith, two men who carried him home, a boy by the river, his answer to his father, a court of poets. Then the Guru steps out before the crowd with a drawn sword.
screen: `ANANDPUR, SPRING 1699.` → `A WEEK THAT BUILDS TO ONE MORNING.` → `A DRAWN SWORD.`

segments.voice: Vaisakhi is the spring harvest festival of Punjab, when the wheat is cut, held in the month of Vaisakh, usually around the middle of April. Long before 1699 it was a time of fairs and gatherings. After 1699 it became something more for Sikhs: the birthday of the Khalsa. Here's what happened, as Sikh tradition tells it. The Guru stood before the crowd, sword raised, and asked a question no one expected. Is there anyone here who will give me their head? Silence. He asked again. Then a third time. Finally one man stood up: Daya Ram, a shopkeeper from Lahore. The Guru took him into a tent. There was a sound. The Guru came out alone, blood on his sword, and asked again. People began to slip away, frightened. Some went to the Guru's mother to complain he'd lost his mind. And still a second man stood. Then a third, a fourth, a fifth. Each went into the tent. Each time the Guru came out alone. What happened inside? The sources don't say clearly, and Sikhs tell it in more than one way. Some tellings say the Guru truly took their lives and restored them. Others say the five were never harmed and the blood was from goats, a test of faith all along. Some Sikhs simply leave the tent closed. What matters is the question, and the five who answered it. Tomorrow, the tent opens.
screen: `VAISAKHI — THE HARVEST FESTIVAL.` · `WHO WILL GIVE ME THEIR HEAD?` · `DAYA RAM STANDS FIRST.` · `FIVE GO INTO THE TENT.` · then, large: `WHO WILL GIVE.`

segments.voice: Let the Guru's question come to you gently, not as a demand: what in your life matters so much you'd give everything for it? A person, a value, a faith, a child. Don't rush an answer; just sit on the hillside with the question, the way the crowd did, and breathe.
Vaisakhi. The spring harvest festival of Punjab, and for Sikhs, the day in 1699 when the Guru asked who would give their head.
Your line: who will give. When the hillside went silent, five stood up. Day eighty-four, the end of another week.

howItsDone: Sikhs celebrate Vaisakhi each April as the birth of the Khalsa, with gurdwara services, processions called nagar kirtan, and, for many, taking amrit on or near the day.
